Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. {{出典の明記|date=2017-01}} '''春日神'''（かすがのかみ）は、[[神道]]の[[神 (神道)|神]]である。春日明神または[[春日権現]]とも称される。[[春日大社]]から[[勧請]]を受けた神のことであり、[[神社]]の祭神を示すときに主祭神と並んで春日大神などと書かれる。春日神を祀る神社は'''春日神社'''などという社名になっており、日本全国に約1000社ある。
== 春日大社の祭神 == 春日神とは、春日大社の祭神である以下の四柱の神の総称である。 * [[タケミカヅチ|武甕槌命]] * [[経津主神|経津主命]] * [[天児屋命|天児屋根命]] * [[比売神]] 武甕槌命（[[鹿島神宮]]）と経津主命（[[香取神宮]]）は[[藤原氏]]（[[中臣氏]]）の守護神とされ、天児屋根命と比売神は藤原氏の祖神とされる。
== 歴史 == 春日大社は[[768年]]に創建された。それ以前の春日の地では本殿廻廊の西南隅にある、摂社・[[榎本神社]]（式内小社）の神が祀られていたとされる。この神は当地の[[地主神]]と考えられ、当地に基盤のあった[[春日氏]]の氏神とされる。江戸時代に祭神は[[サルタヒコ|猿田彦大神]]になったが、それ以前は巨勢姫明神あるいは巨勢祝という神が祀られていたという。
春日大社の四柱の神のうち、当初、特に存在感が高かったのは武甕槌命であるとされる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。天児屋根命は藤原氏の祖神とされるが、大社の創建当時、武甕槌命（鹿島神宮）と経津主命（香取神宮）はともに武神として、中央の政府が蝦夷討伐を進め東北地方への関与を強めていく中で神威が非常に高まっていた{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。両神宮への[[封戸]]の寄進等が盛んとなり、こうした状況が、大社における武甕槌命と経津主命が天児屋根命よりも上座にすえられる結果をもたらしたとされる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。
特に、大社の成立にあたり、鹿島神宮の封戸が最初に大社に与えられていった経緯があり、当初、大社は鹿島神宮の末社であるかのような形態が認められたとされる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。その後、平安時代に入り延暦20年（西暦[[801年]]）からは香取神宮からの援助も受けることとなり、大社における鹿島神宮の圧倒的な存在感は徐々に薄れていったとされる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。「春日大社」を指す際に鹿島や香取といった地名を羅列するような状況もあったが、嘉祥3年（西暦[[850年]]）には「春日大神社」という一つの存在として叙位の文書等に記載されるようになり、四柱の神を包括する大社の独自性が認められるようになっていったとされる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。
それでもなお、大社を鹿島神宮の「末社」的存在とみなす風潮は長期間継続したとされ、『[[大鏡]]』においても、「春日明神（春日神）」とは鹿島の神のことである、と読み取れる記述が見受けられる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。このため、少なくとも、大鏡の成立した11世紀後半までは、「春日神」を「武甕槌命（武甕槌神）」と同一とみなす考えがあったという指摘がある{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。鹿島神宮、武甕槌命の存在感がさらに低下し、四柱の神の総称としての「春日神」が定着したのはその後かなり経ってからであると思われる{{Sfn|重富|1988年}}。
== 全国の主な春日神社 == {{Notice|本節は'''[[Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''の合意による記載基準を元に、 *[[近代社格制度]]下における[[府県社]]以上の神社及び[[神社本庁]]の[[別表神社]] *[[日本国]]の[[文化財保護法]]に基づき国（[[文部科学大臣]]）が指定した文化財を有する神社 *特殊神事が行われる神社 を載せる。
なお、下記以外のものについては「[[春日神社]]」および「[[:Category:春日神社]]」も参照のこと。|section=1}} {{節スタブ}} ===総本社=== *[[春日大社]]（[[奈良県]][[奈良市]]） - 総本社。[[旧官幣大社]]、別表神社。[[重要文化財]]多数所蔵。 ---- ===東北地方=== *春日神社 (利府町)（[[宮城県]][[利府町]]） *春日神社 (鶴岡市)（[[山形県]][[鶴岡市]]櫛引町）- 旧県社。[[黒川能]]が[[重要無形民俗文化財]]。 ===中部地方=== *春日神社 (上越市)（[[新潟県]][[上越市]]春日）-春日大社の記録では全国の春日神社の中で最初に出てくる神社で[[春日山城]]の名称の元になった。 *春日神社 (鯖江市)（[[福井県]][[鯖江市]]鳥井町） - 本殿が[[重要文化財]]。 *[[春日神社 (関市)]]（[[岐阜県]][[関市]]） - 例祭に使用される能装束類（63点）が重要文化財。 ===近畿地方=== *[[桑名宗社]]（[[三重県]][[桑名市]]） - 「[[石取祭]]」が重要無形民俗文化財。 *春日神社 (大津市)（[[滋賀県]][[大津市]]大石富川） - 本殿が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (野洲市)（滋賀県[[野洲市]]） - 神門が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (栗東市)（滋賀県[[栗東市]]） - 表門が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (東近江市)（滋賀県[[東近江市]]小八木町） - 本殿が重要文化財。 *[[大原野神社]]（[[京都府]][[京都市]]） - [[旧官幣中社]]。春日神を[[長岡京]]の近くに勧請したもの。別称は'''京春日'''。 *[[吉田神社]]（京都府京都市） - 旧官幣中社。春日神を[[平安京]]の近くに勧請したもの。 *春日神社 (南丹市)（京都府[[南丹市]]園部町高屋） - 本殿が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (精華町)（京都府[[相楽郡]][[精華町]]菱田宮川原） - 本殿が重要文化財。 *[[枚岡神社]]（[[大阪府]][[東大阪市]]） - 河内国一宮、旧官幣大社。こちらから天児屋根大神と比売大神を春日大社に勧請した、別称は元春日。 *[[倍賀春日神社]]（大阪府[[茨木市]]） - 鎌倉時代の石灯籠が重要文化財。 *[[春日神社 (丹波篠山市)]]（[[兵庫県]][[丹波篠山市]]） - 旧県社。能舞台が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (大和郡山市)（奈良県[[大和郡山市]]矢田町） - [[金剛山寺]]境内にあり、本殿が重要文化財。 *春日神社 (五條市)（奈良県[[五條市]]西吉野町向加名生） - 本殿が重要文化財。 *[[加太春日神社]]（[[和歌山県]][[和歌山市]]） - 本殿が重要文化財。 ===中国地方=== *春日神社 (岡山市北区)（[[岡山県]][[岡山市]][[北区 (岡山市)|北区]]） - 旧県社。 *春日神社 (萩市)（[[山口県]][[萩市]]） - 旧県社。 ===四国地方=== *[[春日神社 (徳島市)]]（[[徳島県]][[徳島市]]） - 旧県社 ===九州地方=== *[[春日神社 (北九州市)]]（[[福岡県]][[北九州市]]） - 旧県社。 *[[春日神社 (春日市)]]（[[福岡県]][[春日市]]） - 「春日の婿押し」が[[重要無形民俗文化財]]。 *[[春日神社 (大分市)|春日神社]]（[[大分県]][[大分市]]） - 旧県社、別表神社。
== 神仏習合 == {{see also|春日権現}} [[本地垂迹]]説では、春日明神の[[本地仏]]には[[不空羂索観音]]があてられ、[[観音菩薩]]の化身とされた。<ref>[[羽田守快]] 『あなたを幸せにみちびく 観音さま ―その教えと信仰の秘訣―』 大法輪閣、2014年、p. 112</ref>

Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} | cult_center ={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}} | symbols = | consort = | parents = | siblings = | 2children = {{ill|Amenotaneko|ja|天種子命|en}} | texts = | 2mother = {{ill|Himegami|en}} | 2father = {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}Shibata, Joue. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}, the second to {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, the third to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Amenokoyane no mikoto|en}}, and the final hall is attributed to the consort, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite web|title=Main Sanctuary|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624041142/http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|archive-date=2019-06-24|access-date=2019-03-28|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp}} Wakamiya Shrine is dedicated to the fifth new member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}.https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/common/001559851.pdf{{Cite web|title=Wakamiya Shrine {{!}} Search Details|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en/H30-00882.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=Japan Tourism Agency,Japan Tourism Agency|language=en}} The two kami {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}} were ''{{ill|bunrei|en}}'' transferred from {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}}, and the shrine was thus given the name of ''Moto-Kasuga'' ("former Kasuga").{{cite book|title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido|last1=Yoshiki|first1=Emi|date=2007|publisher=PHP Institute|isbn=978-4569669304|language=Japanese}}{{cite book|title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri|last1=Okada|first1=Shoji|date=2014|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4582945614|language=Japanese}} Those two deities and their son {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} are ancestors of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}} and {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}.Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}} is located in the western foothills of the {{ill|Mount Ikoma|lt=Ikoma Mountains|en}} in central [[Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]]. In its earliest days, it was a center for [[mountain worship|mountain worship]] and the ''[[kami|kami]]'' of Kozudake, the peak immediately behind the shrine, came to be identified with {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}}, the ancestors of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}. [[ja:春日神]] == Components == He has five components each of which has a corresponding Buddha. Four original members and then the fifth member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}. [[fr:Kasuga-no-Kami]] {| class="wikitable" |+ !Shrine facility ![[Shinto]] part ![[Buddhist]] part |- |first hall |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|4=fr|lt=Takemikazuchi-o}} |{{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu/bitstream/1808/17426/1/Fowler.pdf |- |second hall |{{ill|Futsunushi|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}} |- |third hall |{{ill|Ame no Koyane|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}} |- |fourth hall |{{ill|Himegami|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|4=fr}} |- |Wakamiya Shrine |{{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}} |{{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|en|6=fr}} or {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|4=fr}}.{{Cite journal|last=Giolai|first=Andrea|date=2020-09-22|title=Encounters with the Past: Fractals and Atmospheres at Kasuga Wakamiya Onmatsuri|url=https://brill.com/view/journals/jrj/9/1-3/article-p213_8.xml|journal=Journal of Religion in Japan|volume=9|issue=1-3|pages=213–247|doi=10.1163/22118349-00901002|issn=2211-8349}} |} [[ja:春日神]] [[zh:春日神]] The concept of honji suijaku was also applied to the subsidiary shrines. {| class="wikitable" ! Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. The listed shrines meet the following criteria: * Shrines ranked as provincial or higher under the {{ill|Modern shrine ranking system|ja|近代社格制度}} or listed as {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|ja|神社本庁}}. * Shrines with cultural properties designated by the {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|ja|文化庁}}. * Shrines hosting unique religious rituals. For additional shrines, see {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日神社}} and [[:Category:Kasuga Shrines]].}} {{Stub-section}} === Headquarters === * {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|ja|奈良県}}, {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良市}}) - Headquarters. Former {{ill|Imperial shrine|ja|官幣大社}}, {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}}. Numerous {{ill|Important Cultural Properties of Japan|ja|重要文化財}}. ---- === Tōhoku Region === * Kasuga Shrine (Rifu) ({{ill|Miyagi Prefecture|ja|宮城県}}, {{ill|Rifu|ja|利府町}}) * Kasuga Shrine (Tsuruoka) ({{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|ja|山形県}}, {{ill|Tsuruoka|ja|鶴岡市}}, Kushibiki Town) - Former prefectural shrine. {{ill|Kurokawa nō|ja|黒川能}} is designated as an {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財}}. === Chūbu Region === * Kasuga Shrine (Joetsu) ({{ill|Niigata Prefecture|ja|新潟県}}, {{ill|Joetsu|ja|上越市}}, Kasuga) - Mentioned in the records of Kasuga Taisha as the first Kasuga Shrine in Japan, the namesake of {{ill|Kasugayama Castle|ja|春日山城}}. * Kasuga Shrine (Sabae) ({{ill|Fukui Prefecture|ja|福井県}}, {{ill|Sabae|ja|鯖江市}}, Toriicho) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Seki)|ja|春日神社 (関市)}} ({{ill|Gifu Prefecture|ja|岐阜県}}, {{ill|Seki|ja|関市}}) - Festival costumes (63 items) designated as Important Cultural Properties. === Kinki Region === * {{ill|Kuwana Sōsha|ja|桑名宗社}} ({{ill|Mie Prefecture|ja|三重県}}, {{ill|Kuwana|ja|桑名市}}) - {{ill|Ishidori Matsuri|ja|石取祭}} is designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Ōtsu) ({{ill|Shiga Prefecture|ja|滋賀県}}, {{ill|Ōtsu|ja|大津市}}, Ōishi-Tomigawa) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Yasu) (Shiga Prefecture, {{ill|Yasu|ja|野洲市}}) - Shrine gate designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Rittō) (Shiga Prefecture, {{ill|Rittō|ja|栗東市}}) - Front gate designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Higashiōmi) (Shiga Prefecture, {{ill|Higashiōmi|ja|東近江市}}, Koyagi Town) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Ōharano Shrine|ja|大原野神社}} ({{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|ja|京都府}}, {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都市}}) - Former {{ill|Imperial shrine|ja|官幣中社}}, established near {{ill|Nagaokakyō|ja|長岡京}}. Also known as "Kyō Kasuga." * {{ill|Yoshida Shrine|ja|吉田神社}} (Kyoto Prefecture, Kyoto City) - Former Imperial shrine. Enshrined Kasuga deities near {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}. * Kasuga Shrine (Nantan) (Kyoto Prefecture, {{ill|Nantan|ja|南丹市}}, Sonobe Town, Takaya) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Seika) (Kyoto Prefecture, {{ill|Seika|ja|精華町}}, Hishida-Miyakawara) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|ja|枚岡神社}} ({{ill|Osaka Prefecture|ja|大阪府}}, {{ill|Higashiōsaka|ja|東大阪市}}) - {{ill|Ichinomiya|ja|一宮}} of Kawachi Province, former Imperial shrine. Source of the deities {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根大神}} and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売大神}} for Kasuga Taisha. Also known as "Moto Kasuga." * {{ill|Baiga Kasuga Shrine|ja|倍賀春日神社}} (Osaka Prefecture, {{ill|Ibaraki|ja|茨木市}}) - Kamakura-period stone lantern designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Tamba-Sasayama)|ja|春日神社 (丹波篠山市)}} ({{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県}}, {{ill|Tamba-Sasayama|ja|丹波篠山市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. Noh stage designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Yamatokōriyama) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Yamatokōriyama|ja|大和郡山市}}, Yada Town) - Located in the precincts of {{ill|Kongōzanji|ja|金剛山寺}}, main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Gojō) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Gojō|ja|五條市}}, Nishiyoshino Town, Mukai-Kanau) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kada Kasuga Shrine|ja|加太春日神社}} ({{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, {{ill|Wakayama|ja|和歌山市}}) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. === Chūgoku Region === * Kasuga Shrine (Okayama City, Kita Ward) ({{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県}}, {{ill|Okayama|ja|岡山市}}, {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区}}) - Former prefectural shrine. * Kasuga Shrine (Hagi) ({{ill|Yamaguchi Prefecture|ja|山口県}}, {{ill|Hagi|ja|萩市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. === Shikoku Region === * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Tokushima)|ja|春日神社 (徳島市)}} ({{ill|Tokushima Prefecture|ja|徳島県}}, {{ill|Tokushima|ja|徳島市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. === Kyūshū Region === * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Kitakyūshū)|ja|春日神社 (北九州市)}} ({{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県}}, {{ill|Kitakyūshū|ja|北九州市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Kasuga)|ja|春日神社 (春日市)}} (Fukuoka Prefecture, {{ill|Kasuga|ja|春日市}}) - Known for "Kasuga no Mukooshi," designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|ja|春日神社 (大分市)}} ({{ill|Ōita Prefecture|ja|大分県}}, {{ill|Ōita|ja|大分市}}) - Former prefectural shrine, {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}}. == Syncretism == {{see also|Kasuga Gongen}} Under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework, the Kasuga deity (Kasuga Myōjin) was identified with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, an incarnation of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音菩薩}}.羽田守快『あなたを幸せにみちびく　観音さま』大法輪閣、2014年、p.112. Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} | cult_center ={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}} | symbols = | consort = | parents = | siblings = | 2children = {{ill|Amenotaneko|ja|天種子命|en}} | texts = | 2mother = {{ill|Himegami|en}} | 2father = {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''.
