(1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. Also known as "Moto Kasuga." * {{ill|Baiga Kasuga Shrine|ja|倍賀春日神社}} (Osaka Prefecture, {{ill|Ibaraki|ja|茨木市}}) - Kamakura-period stone lantern designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Tamba-Sasayama)|ja|春日神社 (丹波篠山市)}} ({{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|ja|兵庫県}}, {{ill|Tamba-Sasayama|ja|丹波篠山市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. Noh stage designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Yamatokōriyama) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Yamatokōriyama|ja|大和郡山市}}, Yada Town) - Located in the precincts of {{ill|Kongōzanji|ja|金剛山寺}}, main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Gojō) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Gojō|ja|五條市}}, Nishiyoshino Town, Mukai-Kanau) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kada Kasuga Shrine|ja|加太春日神社}} ({{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, {{ill|Wakayama|ja|和歌山市}}) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. === Chūgoku Region === * Kasuga Shrine (Okayama City, Kita Ward) ({{ill|Okayama Prefecture|ja|岡山県}}, {{ill|Okayama|ja|岡山市}}, {{ill|Kita-ku (Okayama)|ja|北区}}) - Former prefectural shrine. * Kasuga Shrine (Hagi) ({{ill|Yamaguchi Prefecture|ja|山口県}}, {{ill|Hagi|ja|萩市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. === Shikoku Region === * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Tokushima)|ja|春日神社 (徳島市)}} ({{ill|Tokushima Prefecture|ja|徳島県}}, {{ill|Tokushima|ja|徳島市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. === Kyūshū Region === * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Kitakyūshū)|ja|春日神社 (北九州市)}} ({{ill|Fukuoka Prefecture|ja|福岡県}}, {{ill|Kitakyūshū|ja|北九州市}}) - Former prefectural shrine. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Kasuga)|ja|春日神社 (春日市)}} (Fukuoka Prefecture, {{ill|Kasuga|ja|春日市}}) - Known for "Kasuga no Mukooshi," designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|ja|春日神社 (大分市)}} ({{ill|Ōita Prefecture|ja|大分県}}, {{ill|Ōita|ja|大分市}}) - Former prefectural shrine, {{ill|Beppyo Shrine|ja|別表神社}}. == Syncretism == {{see also|Kasuga Gongen}} Under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework, the Kasuga deity (Kasuga Myōjin) was identified with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, an incarnation of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音菩薩}}.羽田守快『あなたを幸せにみちびく　観音さま』大法輪閣、2014年、p.112. Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} | cult_center ={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}} | symbols = | consort = | parents = | siblings = | 2children = {{ill|Amenotaneko|ja|天種子命|en}} | texts = | 2mother = {{ill|Himegami|en}} | 2father = {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}, the second to {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, the third to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Amenokoyane no mikoto|en}}, and the final hall is attributed to the consort, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite web|title=Main Sanctuary|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624041142/http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|archive-date=2019-06-24|access-date=2019-03-28|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp}} Wakamiya Shrine is dedicated to the fifth new member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}.https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/common/001559851.pdf{{Cite web|title=Wakamiya Shrine {{!}} Search Details|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en/H30-00882.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=Japan Tourism Agency,Japan Tourism Agency|language=en}} The two kami {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}} were ''{{ill|bunrei|en}}'' transferred from {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}}, and the shrine was thus given the name of ''Moto-Kasuga'' ("former Kasuga").{{cite book|title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido|last1=Yoshiki|first1=Emi|date=2007|publisher=PHP Institute|isbn=978-4569669304|language=Japanese}}{{cite book|title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri|last1=Okada|first1=Shoji|date=2014|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4582945614|language=Japanese}} Those two deities and their son {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} are ancestors of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}} and {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}.Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}} is located in the western foothills of the {{ill|Mount Ikoma|lt=Ikoma Mountains|en}} in central [[Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]]. In its earliest days, it was a center for [[mountain worship|mountain worship]] and the ''[[kami|kami]]'' of Kozudake, the peak immediately behind the shrine, came to be identified with {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}}, the ancestors of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}. [[ja:春日神]] == Components == He has five components each of which has a corresponding Buddha. Four original members and then the fifth member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}. [[fr:Kasuga-no-Kami]] {| class="wikitable" |+ !Shrine facility ![[Shinto]] part ![[Buddhist]] part |- |first hall |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|4=fr|lt=Takemikazuchi-o}} |{{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu/bitstream/1808/17426/1/Fowler.pdf |- |second hall |{{ill|Futsunushi|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}} |- |third hall |{{ill|Ame no Koyane|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}} |- |fourth hall |{{ill|Himegami|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|4=fr}} |- |Wakamiya Shrine |{{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}} |{{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|en|6=fr}} or {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|4=fr}}.{{Cite journal|last=Giolai|first=Andrea|date=2020-09-22|title=Encounters with the Past: Fractals and Atmospheres at Kasuga Wakamiya Onmatsuri|url=https://brill.com/view/journals/jrj/9/1-3/article-p213_8.xml|journal=Journal of Religion in Japan|volume=9|issue=1-3|pages=213–247|doi=10.1163/22118349-00901002|issn=2211-8349}} |} [[ja:春日神]] [[zh:春日神]] The concept of honji suijaku was also applied to the subsidiary shrines. {| class="wikitable" ! Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}, the second to {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, the third to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Amenokoyane no mikoto|en}}, and the final hall is attributed to the consort, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite web|title=Main Sanctuary|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624041142/http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|archive-date=2019-06-24|access-date=2019-03-28|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp}} Wakamiya Shrine is dedicated to the fifth new member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}.https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/common/001559851.pdf{{Cite web|title=Wakamiya Shrine {{!}} Search Details|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en/H30-00882.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=Japan Tourism Agency,Japan Tourism Agency|language=en}} The two kami {{ill|Ame no Koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}} were ''{{ill|bunrei|en}}'' transferred from {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}}, and the shrine was thus given the name of ''Moto-Kasuga'' ("former Kasuga").{{cite book|title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido|last1=Yoshiki|first1=Emi|date=2007|publisher=PHP Institute|isbn=978-4569669304|language=Japanese}}{{cite book|title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri|last1=Okada|first1=Shoji|date=2014|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4582945614|language=Japanese}} Those two deities and their son {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} are ancestors of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}} and {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}.Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en}} is located in the western foothills of the {{ill|Mount Ikoma|lt=Ikoma Mountains|en}} in central [[Osaka Prefecture|Osaka Prefecture]]. In its earliest days, it was a center for [[mountain worship|mountain worship]] and the ''[[kami|kami]]'' of Kozudake, the peak immediately behind the shrine, came to be identified with {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en}}, the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en}}, the ancestors of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en}}. [[ja:春日神]] == Components == He has five components each of which has a corresponding Buddha. Four original members and then the fifth member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}. [[fr:Kasuga-no-Kami]] {| class="wikitable" |+ !Shrine facility ![[Shinto]] part ![[Buddhist]] part |- |first hall |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|4=fr|lt=Takemikazuchi-o}} |{{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu/bitstream/1808/17426/1/Fowler.pdf |- |second hall |{{ill|Futsunushi|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}} |- |third hall |{{ill|Ame no Koyane|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}} |- |fourth hall |{{ill|Himegami|en|4=fr}} |{{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|4=fr}} |- |Wakamiya Shrine |{{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}} |{{ill|Manjushri|ja|文殊菩薩|en|6=fr}} or {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|4=fr}}.{{Cite journal|last=Giolai|first=Andrea|date=2020-09-22|title=Encounters with the Past: Fractals and Atmospheres at Kasuga Wakamiya Onmatsuri|url=https://brill.com/view/journals/jrj/9/1-3/article-p213_8.xml|journal=Journal of Religion in Japan|volume=9|issue=1-3|pages=213–247|doi=10.1163/22118349-00901002|issn=2211-8349}} |} [[ja:春日神]] [[zh:春日神]] The concept of honji suijaku was also applied to the subsidiary shrines. {| class="wikitable" ! Former Title !! Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha}} {{complex}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|lt=chigi|en}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first mikoto|en}}, and the final hall is attributed to the consort, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami}}.{{Cite web|title=Main Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|ja|弥勒菩薩}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|ja|毘沙門天}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|ja|虚空蔵菩薩}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|ja|不動明王}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|ja|阿弥陀如来}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|syncretic deity|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara |id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha }}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|ja|十一面観音}} as its {{ill|honji-butsu|ja|本地仏}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|タケミカヅチ}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主神}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋命}}, and {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}). As {{ill|shinbutsu shūgō|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|ja|長岡京}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|ja|平安京}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|ja|興福寺}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|jingū-ji|ja|神宮寺}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|ja|権現}} under the {{ill|honji suijaku|ja|本地垂迹}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|ja|貞慶|lt=Jōkei}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Śākyamuni|ja|釈迦如来}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|ja|春日権現験記}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|ja|法相宗|lt=Hossō sect}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Mount Kasuga|ja|春日山}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|ja|廃仏毀釈}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became {{ill|Shinto priests|ja|神職}} at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). [[Category:Gongen]] [[Category:Kasuga Shrines]] [[Category:Kasuga Taisha]] [[Category:Japanese deities]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Kṣitigarbha]] [[ja:春日権現]] == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|kami|ja|神 (神道)}} in {{ill|Shinto|ja|神道}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} * {{ill|Himegami|ja|比売神}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|ja|中臣氏}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|ujigami|ja|氏神}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|ja|768年}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Chinjugami|ja|地主神}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|ja|藤原氏}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島神宮}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|ja|香取神宮}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|ja|蝦夷}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|ja|大鏡}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''.
