Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|en|Maitreya|WD=Q193461|lt=Maitreya|1=Maitreya}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|en|Vaiśravaṇa|WD=Q866315|lt=Vaiśravaṇa|1=Vaiśravaṇa}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Ākāśagarbha|1=Ākāśagarbha}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|en|Acala|WD=Q337624|lt=Fudō Myōō|1=Acala}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitābha|1=Amitābha}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara|id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|qq=}}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bhaisajyaguru|qq=}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kṣitigarbha|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|WD=Q11404731|lt=Ekādaśamukha|1=Ekādaśamukha}} as its {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=Honji Buddha|1=Honji suijaku}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|WD=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|Takemikazuchi|WD=Q1502690|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|1=Takemikazuchi}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|en|Futsunushi|WD=Q1107286|WD=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi|1=Futsunushi}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|Ame-no-Koyane|WD=Q2564508|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, and {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|WD=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|WD=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}). As {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|en|Nagaoka-kyō|WD=Q1052803|lt=Nagaoka-kyō|1=Nagaoka-kyō}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō|1=Heian-kyō}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nara|qq=}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|en|Kōfuku-ji|WD=Q1070863|lt=Kōfuku-ji|1=Kōfuku-ji}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lotus Eight Lectures|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鹿島神宮}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katori Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Mikasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春日山 (奈良県)|1=Mount Kasuga|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513602}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|en|Gongen|WD=Q3080343|lt=Gongen|1=Gongen}} under the {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|en|Jōkei (monk)|WD=Q11634518|lt=Jōkei|1=Jōkei (monk)}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata|qq=}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|en|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|WD=Q6374869|lt=Kasuga Gongen Genki E|1=Kasuga Gongen Genki E}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yogācāra|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 成唯識論|1=Cheng Weishi Lun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q848906}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Hossō sect|1=East Asian Yogācāra}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Mandalas|qq=}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Kasugayama|en|Kasugayama|WD=Q11513600|lt=Mount Kasuga|1=Kasugayama}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration|1=Meiji Restoration}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|WD=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became [[:en:Kannushi|Shinto priests]] at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|Kami|en|Kami|WD=Q524158|lt=kami|1=Kami}} in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Gongen|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|Bunrei|en|Bunrei|WD=Q195793|lt=Enshrinement|1=Bunrei}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} * {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|WD=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|WD=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|WD=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|WD=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|Ujigami|en|Ujigami|WD=Q767655|lt=ujigami|1=Ujigami}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513639}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose Hime Myōjin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose no Iwai|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|WD=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fūko|qq=}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|lt=Massha|1=Setsumatsusha|2=ja|3=摂末社|4=zh|5=攝末社|6=es|7=Setsumatsusha|8=fr|9=Setsumatsusha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/branch shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 摂末社}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|en|768|WD=Q29961|lt=768|1=768}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Landlord deity|en|Landlord deity|WD=Q4160872|lt=Chinjugami|1=Landlord deity}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513639}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ|1=Takemikazuchi}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|WD=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|WD=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神|1=Futsunushi}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|WD=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|WD=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fuko|1=Fūko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11458391}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court Ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. The listed shrines meet the following criteria: * Shrines Ranked as provincial or higher under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|en|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|WD=Q712534|lt=Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} or listed as {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|WD=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}. * Shrines with cultural properties designated by the {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|en|Agency for Cultural Affairs|WD=Q1009519|lt=Agency for Cultural Affairs|1=Agency for Cultural Affairs}}. * Shrines hosting unique religious rituals. For additional shrines, see {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|lt=Kasuga-taisha|lt=Kasuga Shrine|ja|春日神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Shrine|qq=}} and .}} {{Stub-section}} === Headquarters === * {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}} ({{ill|Nara Prefecture|en|Nara Prefecture|WD=Q131287|lt=Nara Prefecture|1=Nara Prefecture}}, {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}}) - Headquarters. Former {{ill|Imperial shrine|ja|官幣大社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial shrine|1=Kanpei Taisha (disambiguation)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10209769}}, {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}}. Former Prefectural shrine. {{ill|Ogisai Kurokawa Noh|en|Ogisai Kurokawa Noh|WD=Q6374036|lt=Kurokawa nō|1=Ogisai Kurokawa Noh}} is designated as an {{ill|Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|ja|重要無形民俗文化財|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|1=National Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q6573893}}. === Chūbu Region === * Kasuga Shrine (Joetsu) ({{ill|Niigata Prefecture|en|Niigata Prefecture|WD=Q132705|lt=Niigata Prefecture|1=Niigata Prefecture}}, {{ill|Jōetsu, Niigata|en|Jōetsu, Niigata|WD=Q582289|lt=Joetsu|1=Jōetsu, Niigata}}, Kasuga) - Enshrined Kasuga deities near {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō|1=Heian-kyō}}. * Kasuga Shrine (Nantan) (Kyoto Prefecture, {{ill|Nantan, Kyoto|en|Nantan, Kyoto|WD=Q170421|lt=Nantan|1=Nantan, Kyoto}}, Sonobe Town, Takaya) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Seika) (Kyoto Prefecture, {{ill|Seika, Kyoto|en|Seika, Kyoto|WD=Q1203237|lt=Seika|1=Seika, Kyoto}}, Hishida-Miyakawara) - Main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en|Hiraoka Shrine|WD=Q32422|lt=Hiraoka Shrine|1=Hiraoka Shrine}} ({{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|WD=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture|1=Osaka Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashiōsaka|en|Higashiōsaka|WD=Q243863|lt=Higashiōsaka|1=Higashiōsaka}}) - {{ill|Ichinomiya|en|Ichinomiya|WD=Q1656379|lt=Ichinomiya|1=Ichinomiya}} of Kawachi Province, former Imperial shrine. Noh stage designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Yamatokōriyama) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Yamatokōriyama|en|Yamatokōriyama|WD=Q118213|lt=Yamatokōriyama|1=Yamatokōriyama}}, Yada Town) - Located in the precincts of {{ill|Kongōzanji|ja|金剛山寺|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kongōzanji|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 矢田寺|1=Yata-dera Temple|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1781626}}, main hall designated as an Important Cultural Property. * Kasuga Shrine (Gojō) (Nara Prefecture, {{ill|Gojō, Nara|en|Gojō, Nara|WD=Q602571|lt=Gojō|1=Gojō, Nara}}, Nishiyoshino Town, Mukai-Kanau) - Former Prefectural shrine. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Kasuga)|ja|春日神社 (春日市)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Shrine (Kasuga)|qq=}} (Fukuoka Prefecture, {{ill|Kasuga, Fukuoka|en|Kasuga, Fukuoka|WD=Q47084|lt=Kasuga|1=Kasuga, Fukuoka}}) - Known for "Kasuga no Mukooshi," designated as an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property. * {{ill|Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|ja|春日神社 (大分市)|1=Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Shrine (Ōita)|qq=}} ({{ill|Ōita Prefecture|en|Ōita Prefecture|WD=Q133924|lt=Ōita Prefecture|1=Ōita Prefecture}}, {{ill|Ōita (city)|en|Ōita (city)|WD=Q199609|lt=Ōita|1=Ōita (city)}}) - Former Prefectural shrine, {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}}. == Syncretism == {{see also|Kasuga Gongen}} Under the {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} framework, the Kasuga deity (Kasuga Myōjin) was identified with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara|id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|qq=}}, an incarnation of {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Kannon|1=Avalokiteśvara}}.羽田守快『あなたを幸せにみちびく　観音さま』大法輪閣、2014th year 、p.112. == In Popular culture == Kasuga-no-Kami, Jade Angel is a card in {{ill|WIXOSS|en|4=ja|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/WIXOSS|qq=}}. Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}} | cult_center ={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}}|symbols = | consort = | parents = | siblings = | 2children = {{ill|Amenotaneko|ja|天種子命|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amenotaneko|qq=}} | texts = | 2mother = {{ill|Himegami|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}|2father = {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}}Shibata, Joue. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha| attributes ={{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|WD=Q2564508|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}; {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|WD=Q91088537|1=Ame-no-Oshikumone}}; {{ill|Futsunushi|WD=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}}; {{ill|Himegami|WD=Q22070227|1=Himegami}}; {{ill|Takemikazuchi|WD=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi}}| equivalent5_type = Japanese | equivalent5 ={{ill|Kasuga Gongen|WD=Q11088804|1=Kasuga Gongen}}}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gongen|qq=}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|WD=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|qq=|1=Futsunushi}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|qq=|1=Takemikazuchi}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buddhism|qq=}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kami|qq=}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-zukuri|qq=}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/katsuogi|qq=}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|en|Chigi (architecture)|WD=Q262282|lt=Chigi (architecture)|1=Chigi (architecture)}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|en|Maitreya|WD=Q193461|lt=Maitreya|1=Maitreya}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|en|Vaiśravaṇa|WD=Q866315|lt=Vaiśravaṇa|1=Vaiśravaṇa}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|WD=Q416174|lt=Ākāśagarbha|1=Ākāśagarbha}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|en|Acala|WD=Q337624|lt=Fudō Myōō|1=Acala}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|WD=Q236242|lt=Amitābha|1=Amitābha}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara|id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|qq=}}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bhaisajyaguru|qq=}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kṣitigarbha|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|WD=Q11404731|lt=Ekādaśamukha|1=Ekādaśamukha}} as its {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=Honji Buddha|1=Honji suijaku}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|WD=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|Takemikazuchi|WD=Q1502690|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|1=Takemikazuchi}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|en|Futsunushi|WD=Q1107286|WD=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi|1=Futsunushi}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|Ame-no-Koyane|WD=Q2564508|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, and {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|WD=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|WD=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}). As {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|WD=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|en|Nagaoka-kyō|WD=Q1052803|lt=Nagaoka-kyō|1=Nagaoka-kyō}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|WD=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō|1=Heian-kyō}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nara|qq=}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q740246}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|en|Kōfuku-ji|WD=Q1070863|lt=Kōfuku-ji|1=Kōfuku-ji}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lotus Eight Lectures|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鹿島神宮}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katori Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Mikasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春日山 (奈良県)|1=Mount Kasuga|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513602}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|en|Gongen|WD=Q3080343|lt=Gongen|1=Gongen}} under the {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|WD=Q3080781|lt=honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|en|Jōkei (monk)|WD=Q11634518|lt=Jōkei|1=Jōkei (monk)}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata|qq=}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|en|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|WD=Q6374869|lt=Kasuga Gongen Genki E|1=Kasuga Gongen Genki E}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yogācāra|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 成唯識論|1=Cheng Weishi Lun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q848906}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|WD=Q349849|lt=Hossō sect|1=East Asian Yogācāra}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Mandalas|qq=}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Kasugayama|en|Kasugayama|WD=Q11513600|lt=Mount Kasuga|1=Kasugayama}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|WD=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration|1=Meiji Restoration}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|WD=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|WD=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became [[:en:Kannushi|Shinto priests]] at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|Kami|en|Kami|WD=Q524158|lt=kami|1=Kami}} in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|WD=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Gongen|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|Bunrei|en|Bunrei|WD=Q195793|lt=Enshrinement|1=Bunrei}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} * {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|WD=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|WD=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|WD=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|WD=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|Ujigami|en|Ujigami|WD=Q767655|lt=ujigami|1=Ujigami}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513639}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose Hime Myōjin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose no Iwai|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|WD=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fūko|qq=}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|lt=Massha|1=Setsumatsusha|2=ja|3=摂末社|4=zh|5=攝末社|6=es|7=Setsumatsusha|8=fr|9=Setsumatsusha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/branch shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 摂末社}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|WD=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|en|768|WD=Q29961|lt=768|1=768}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Landlord deity|en|Landlord deity|WD=Q4160872|lt=Chinjugami|1=Landlord deity}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513639}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|WD=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ|1=Takemikazuchi}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|WD=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|WD=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|WD=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神|1=Futsunushi}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|WD=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|WD=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fuko|1=Fūko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11458391}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court Ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|WD=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|qq=|1=Futsunushi}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|qq=|1=Takemikazuchi}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buddhism|qq=}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kami|qq=}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-zukuri|qq=}}. Honji-Butsu |- | Sanjūhassho || {{ill|Maitreya|en|Maitreya|qid=Q193461|lt=Maitreya|1=Maitreya}} |- | Enomoto || {{ill|Vaiśravaṇa|en|Vaiśravaṇa|qid=Q866315|lt=Vaiśravaṇa|1=Vaiśravaṇa}} |- | Ki-no-Yashiro || {{ill|Ākāśagarbha|en|Ākāśagarbha|qid=Q416174|lt=Ākāśagarbha|1=Ākāśagarbha}} |- | Hitokotonushi || {{ill|Acala|en|Acala|qid=Q337624|lt=Fudō Myōō|1=Acala}} |- | Haraedo || {{ill|Amitābha|en|Amitābha|qid=Q236242|lt=Amitābha|1=Amitābha}} |} == History == '''Kasuga Gongen''' (春日権現) is a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|qid=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} in Japanese religion, associated with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara|id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|qq=}}, {{ill|Bhaisajyaguru|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bhaisajyaguru|qq=}}, {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|4=fr|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kṣitigarbha|qq=}}, and {{ill|Ekādaśamukha|en|Ekādaśamukha|qid=Q11404731|lt=Ekādaśamukha|1=Ekādaśamukha}} as its {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|qid=Q3080781|lt=Honji Buddha|1=Honji suijaku}}. Kasuga Gongen is also referred to as "Kasuga Daimyōjin" (春日大明神). Before the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|qid=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|qid=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} policies during the Meiji Restoration, Kasuga Gongen was enshrined at sites such as {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|qid=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}}. Kasuga Shrine enshrines four deities: {{ill|Takemikazuchi|en|Takemikazuchi|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|1=Takemikazuchi}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|en|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi|1=Futsunushi}}, {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|Ame-no-Koyane|qid=Q2564508|lt=Ame-no-Koyane|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, and {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|qid=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}}, with Ame-no-Koyane being the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|qid=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|qid=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}). As {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|en|Shinbutsu-shūgō|qid=Q2279088|lt=Shinbutsu-shūgō|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}} progressed, and as the capital moved from {{ill|Nagaoka-kyō|en|Nagaoka-kyō|qid=Q1052803|lt=Nagaoka-kyō|1=Nagaoka-kyō}} to {{ill|Heian-kyō|en|Heian-kyō|qid=Q751907|lt=Heian-kyō|1=Heian-kyō}}, the political influence of the Fujiwara clan shifted from {{ill|Nara|ja|奈良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nara|qq=}} to {{ill|Kyoto|ja|京都|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto|1=Kyōto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q740246}}. During this time, {{ill|Kōfuku-ji|en|Kōfuku-ji|qid=Q1070863|lt=Kōfuku-ji|1=Kōfuku-ji}}, the Fujiwara clan's family temple, became the {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|qid=Q1074971|lt=jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}} (guardian temple) of Kasuga Shrine and exerted significant control over it, effectively incorporating it into the temple's estate. Starting in 1018 (Kan'nin 2), Kōfuku-ji priests began holding {{ill|Lotus Eight Lectures|ja|法華八講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lotus Eight Lectures|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} at Kasuga Shrine, increasing the site’s Buddhist influence. According to traditions, the deities of {{ill|Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Jingū|lt=Kashima Shrine|ja|鹿島大明神|Kashima Daimyōjin=Kashima Daimyōjin|lt=Kashima Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashima Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 鹿島神宮}} (Takemikazuchi) and {{ill|Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Jingū|lt=Katori Shrine|ja|香取大明神|lt=Katori Daimyōjin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katori Shrine|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Futsunushi) were said to have been transferred to {{ill|Mount Mikasa|ja|御蓋山|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Mikasa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春日山 (奈良県)|1=Mount Kasuga|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11513602}} (Mount Wakakusa) for the protection of Buddhist law and state pacification.Kasuga Daimyōjin-ji Consequently, the deities were venerated as {{ill|Gongen|en|Gongen|qid=Q3080343|lt=Gongen|1=Gongen}} under the {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|qid=Q3080781|lt=honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} framework. However, the monk {{ill|Jōkei (monk)|en|Jōkei (monk)|qid=Q11634518|lt=Jōkei|1=Jōkei (monk)}} regarded the deity in the First Hall as {{ill|Shakyamuni Tathāgata|ja|釈迦如来|1=Shakyamuni Tathāgata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shakyamuni Tathāgata|qq=}}. The {{ill|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|en|Kasuga Gongen Genki E|qid=Q6374869|lt=Kasuga Gongen Genki E|1=Kasuga Gongen Genki E}} stated that those studying {{ill|Yogācāra|ja|唯識論|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yogācāra|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 成唯識論|1=Cheng Weishi Lun|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q848906}} in the {{ill|East Asian Yogācāra|en|East Asian Yogācāra|qid=Q349849|lt=Hossō sect|1=East Asian Yogācāra}} were protected by Kasuga Gongen. The creation of {{ill|Kasuga Mandalas|ja|春日曼荼羅|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Mandalas|qq=}} also flourished, depicting the honji-butsu of the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and subsidiary shrines like Wakamiya. {{gallery |width=200 |lines=6 |file:detail of Japanese Kasuga Mandala, Nambokucho period, ink colors and gold on silk.jpg|Kasuga Mandala (Nanboku-chō period)
Depicts the four deities enshrined in the main halls (First to Fourth Halls) and Wakamiya against the backdrop of {{ill|Kasugayama|en|Kasugayama|qid=Q11513600|lt=Mount Kasuga|1=Kasugayama}}. |file:Kasugamandala detail.jpg|A Kasuga Mandala aligning deities with their honji-butsu.
Top row: the Four Halls. Bottom row (left to right): Enomoto, Ki-no-Yashiro, Sanjūhassho, Fourth Hall, Second Hall, Third Hall, Wakamiya, Mizutani, Hitokotonushi. }} === Syncretism and Separation === During the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|en|Meiji Restoration|qid=Q8707|lt=Meiji Restoration|1=Meiji Restoration}}, the policies of {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|en|Shinbutsu bunri|qid=Q1970535|lt=Shinbutsu bunri|1=Shinbutsu bunri}} and {{ill|Haibutsu kishaku|en|Haibutsu kishaku|qid=Q702298|lt=Haibutsu kishaku|1=Haibutsu kishaku}} resulted in the abolition of Kasuga Gongen worship. Due to financial difficulties, many monks of Kōfuku-ji renounced their clerical status and became [[:en:Kannushi|Shinto priests]] at Kasuga Shrine. Additionally, the temple’s lands were confiscated by the Meiji government, leading to the separation of Kasuga Shrine from Kōfuku-ji. Kasuga Shrine was renamed Kasuga Taisha (Kasuga Grand Shrine). == Kasuga-no-Kami == '''Kasuga-no-Kami''' (春日神) is a {{ill|Kami|en|Kami|qid=Q524158|lt=kami|1=Kami}} in {{ill|Shinto|en|Shinto|qid=Q812767|lt=Shinto|1=Shinto}}, also referred to as Kasuga Myōjin (春日明神) or {{ill|Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga-no-Kami|lt=Kasuga Gongen|ja|春日権現|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga Gongen|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}. This term refers to the deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|qid=Q714559|lt=Kasuga Shrine|1=Kasuga-taisha}} and other shrines where they were {{ill|Bunrei|en|Bunrei|qid=Q195793|lt=Enshrinement|1=Bunrei}} (enshrined from another location). The name "Kasuga-no-Kami" is used in conjunction with the shrine's main deities, often written as Kasuga Ōkami (春日大神). Shrines dedicated to Kasuga-no-Kami are commonly named "Kasuga Shrine" (春日神社) and number approximately 1,000 across Japan. == Deities of Kasuga Taisha == Kasuga-no-Kami refers collectively to the four deities enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|qid=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}}: * {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ}} * {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神}} * {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} * {{ill|Himegami|en|Himegami|qid=Q22070227|lt=Himegami|1=Himegami}} Takemikazuchi (of {{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|qid=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and Futsunushi (of {{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|qid=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) are considered guardian deities of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|qid=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}} (specifically the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|Nakatomi clan|qid=Q1198447|lt=Nakatomi clan|1=Nakatomi clan}}), while Ame-no-Koyane and Himegami are regarded as ancestral deities of the Fujiwara clan. == History == Kasuga Taisha was founded in 768. Before its establishment, the deity worshipped in the Kasuga area was enshrined at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, located in the southwestern corner of the main hall's corridor. This deity is thought to have been the {{ill|Ujigami|en|Ujigami|qid=Q767655|lt=ujigami|1=Ujigami}} (clan deity) of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11513639}}, who were based in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was identified as {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko Ōkami|lt=Sarutahiko|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, though earlier traditions suggest the deity was {{ill|Kose Hime Myōjin|ja|巨勢姫明神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose Hime Myōjin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} or {{ill|Kose no Iwai|ja|巨勢祝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kose no Iwai|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. Among the four deities, Takemikazuchi held particular prominence at the shrine’s establishment.Shigetomi (1988) While Ame-no-Koyane is regarded as the Fujiwara clan's ancestral deity, during the shrine's founding, Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi were venerated as war deities. These deities gained influence as the central government expanded its control over the Tōhoku region through campaigns against the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}}. Both shrines (Kashima and Katori) received significant offerings of {{ill|fūko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/fūko|qq=}}, enhancing their prominence. This led to Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi being placed in higher positions than Ame-no-Koyane at Kasuga Taisha. Initially, Kasuga Taisha operated as a {{ill|branch shrine|ja|末社|lt=Massha|1=Setsumatsusha|2=ja|3=摂末社|4=zh|5=攝末社|6=es|7=Setsumatsusha|8=fr|9=Setsumatsusha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/branch shrine|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 摂末社}} (branch shrine) of Kashima Shrine, as reflected in historical records. The shrine's ties with Kashima gradually weakened after receiving support from Katori Shrine in 801 (Enryaku 20). By 850 (Kashō 3), documents began referring to Kasuga Taisha as an independent entity, acknowledging its unique identity. However, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as subordinate to Kashima Shrine persisted until the late Heian period. Records from the late 11th century, such as the {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|qid=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, suggest that "Kasuga Myōjin" (Kasuga deity) was synonymous with Takemikazuchi. The recognition of "Kasuga-no-Kami" as encompassing all four deities only solidified much later. == History == {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|Kasuga-taisha|qid=Q714559|lt=Kasuga-taisha|1=Kasuga-taisha}} was established in {{ill|768|en|768|qid=Q29961|lt=768|1=768}}. Prior to its establishment, the deity enshrined in the area of Kasuga was believed to be the tutelary deity of the region. This deity was worshiped at {{ill|Enomoto Shrine|ja|榎本神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Enomoto Shrine|qq=}}, a subordinate shrine located at the southwestern corner of the main shrine's cloister. This deity was regarded as the {{ill|Landlord deity|en|Landlord deity|qid=Q4160872|lt=Chinjugami|1=Landlord deity}} (guardian deity of the land) and considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Kasuga clan|ja|春日氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga clan|1=Kasuga Clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11513639}}, who had a historical presence in the area. During the Edo period, the enshrined deity was changed to {{ill|Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja|猿田彦大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sarutahiko Ōkami|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to サルタヒコ}}, but earlier records suggest that the deity was either Kosehime Myōjin or Koseiwi. Among the four deities of Kasuga Taisha, {{ill|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌命|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to タケミカヅチ|1=Takemikazuchi}} was believed to hold a particularly significant presence at the time of the shrine’s founding. Although {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|ja|天児屋根命|1=Ame-no-Koyane|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天児屋命}} is considered the ancestral deity of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|Fujiwara clan|qid=Q641628|lt=Fujiwara clan|1=Fujiwara clan}}, during the shrine's establishment, Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ({{ill|Kashima Shrine|en|Kashima Shrine|qid=Q706499|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=Kashima Jingū}}) and {{ill|Futsunushi|ja|経津主命|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi-no-Mikoto|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 経津主神|1=Futsunushi}} ({{ill|Katori Shrine|en|Katori Shrine|qid=Q372380|lt=Katori Shrine|1=Katori Jingū}}) were highly venerated as war gods. This was due to the central government’s ongoing efforts to subdue the {{ill|Emishi|en|Emishi|qid=Q932574|lt=Emishi|1=Emishi}} and expand its influence in the northeastern regions of Japan. As a result, their divine authority was greatly elevated at the time.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} The contributions of fiefs ({{ill|Fuko|ja|封戸|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fuko|1=Fūko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11458391}}) to both Kashima and Katori Shrines were actively promoted, which elevated the status of Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto and Futsunushi-no-Mikoto above Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto at Kasuga Taisha.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} During the shrine's establishment, fiefs from Kashima Shrine were initially granted to Kasuga Taisha, effectively positioning Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate shrine of Kashima Shrine. Over time, the overwhelming influence of Kashima Shrine gradually diminished as Katori Shrine began providing support to Kasuga Taisha from 801 CE (20th year of the Enryaku era). By 850 CE (3rd year of the Kashō era), Kasuga Taisha had established its unique identity and was recognized as “Kasuga Daijinja” in official documents conferring court Ranks, signifying its independence as a shrine representing all four deities collectively.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} Nonetheless, the perception of Kasuga Taisha as a subordinate of Kashima Shrine persisted for a long time. In the historical text {{ill|Ōkagami|en|Ōkagami|qid=Q385120|lt=Ōkagami|1=Ōkagami}}, there are references suggesting that "Kasuga Myōjin (Kasuga Deity)" refers specifically to the deity of Kashima.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} This indicates that until the late 11th century, when Ōkagami was compiled, the notion of equating "Kasuga Deity" with "Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto" was still prevalent. The decline in the influence of Kashima Shrine and Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto, and the eventual establishment of "Kasuga Deities" as a collective term for the four gods, is believed to have occurred significantly later.{{Sfn|Shigetomi|1988}} == Major Kasuga Shrines Across Japan == {{Notice|This section is based on the consensus from '''[[:ja:Wikipedia‐ノート:ウィキプロジェクト 神道#神社の一覧記事・一覧形式の例示部分について]]'''. Former Prefectural shrine, {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine|1=Beppyo shrine}}. == Syncretism == {{see also|Kasuga Gongen}} Under the {{ill|Honji suijaku|en|Honji suijaku|qid=Q3080781|lt=honji suijaku|1=Honji suijaku}} framework, the Kasuga deity (Kasuga Myōjin) was identified with {{ill|Amoghapasha|ja|不空羂索観音|fr|Amoghapasha Lokeshvara|id|Arca Amoghapasa|jv|Arca Amoghapasa|zh|不空羂索觀音|simple|User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amoghapasha|qq=}}, an incarnation of {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|qid=Q193849|lt=Kannon|1=Avalokiteśvara}}.羽田守快『あなたを幸せにみちびく　観音さま』大法輪閣、2014th year 、p.112. == In Popular culture == Kasuga-no-Kami, Jade Angel is a card in {{ill|WIXOSS|en|4=ja|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/WIXOSS|qq=}}. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha |cult_centre={{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}}|alt=Kasuga Taisha| attributes ={{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|qid=Q2564508|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}; {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|qid=Q91088537|1=Ame-no-Oshikumone}}; {{ill|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}}; {{ill|Himegami|qid=Q22070227|1=Himegami}}; {{ill|Takemikazuchi|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi}}| equivalent5_type = Japanese | equivalent5 ={{ill|Kasuga Gongen|qid=Q11088804|1=Kasuga Gongen}}}} Kasuga no [[Kami]] ([[:ja:春日神|春日神]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Gongen|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gongen|qq=}} ([[:ja:春日権現|春日権現]]) or Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}} (春日大明神) is a god of {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}}.{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods: a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}}{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|last=Tyler|first=Royall|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} It is composed of five separate deities each with a [[Shinto|Shinto]] and a Buddhist equivalent. He is considered the protector deity of [[Nara]] and the [[Fujiwara clan]].https://www.japanhousela.com/exhibitions/nature-supernature/supernature-spiritual-forces-in-the-japanese-landscape-kami/ The four main [[kami|kami]] enshrined at {{ill|Kasuga-taisha|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-taisha|qq=}} are {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}}, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}, {{ill|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|qq=|1=Futsunushi}}, and {{ill|Takemikazuchi|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|qq=|1=Takemikazuchi}}. Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|lt=syncretic|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinbutsu-shūgō|qq=}}, combined deity known as Kasuga {{ill|Myōjin|lt=Daimyōjin|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Myōjin|qq=}}. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a {{ill|Buddhism|lt=Buddhist|lt=Buddhist|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Buddhism|qq=}} deity and Shinto kami counterpart. The fifth deity, {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|lt=Ame no koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once.{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} The four main {{ill|kami|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/kami|qq=}} (excluding {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}) each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same {{ill|Kasuga-zukuri|lt=architectural style|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasuga-zukuri|qq=}}. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, {{ill|katsuogi|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/katsuogi|qq=}} (decorative logs), and {{ill|Chigi (architecture)|en|Chigi (architecture)|qid=Q262282|lt=Chigi (architecture)|1=Chigi (architecture)}} (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines: a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|last=Cali|first=Joseph|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to {{ill|Takemikazuchi|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takemikazuchi|qq=|1=Takemikazuchi}}, the second to {{ill|Futsunushi|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futsunushi no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Futsunushi|qq=|1=Futsunushi}}, the third to {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amenokoyane no mikoto|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=|1=Ame-no-Koyane}}, and the final hall is attributed to the consort, {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}}.{{Cite web|title=Main Sanctuary|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190624041142/http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|archive-date=2019-06-24|access-date=2019-03-28|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp}} Wakamiya Shrine is dedicated to the fifth new member {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|en|Draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}.https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/common/001559851.pdf{{Cite web|title=Wakamiya Shrine {{!}} Search Details|url=https://www.mlit.go.jp/tagengo-db/en/H30-00882.html|access-date=2024-03-20|website=Japan Tourism Agency,Japan Tourism Agency|language=en}} The two kami {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame no Koyane|qq=}} and {{ill|Himegami|en|4=simple|5=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himegami|qq=}} were ''{{ill|bunrei|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/bunrei|qq=}}'' transferred from {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hiraoka Shrine|qq=}}, and the shrine was thus given the name of ''Moto-Kasuga'' ("former Kasuga").{{cite book|title=Zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' tettei gaido|last1=Yoshiki|first1=Emi|date=2007|publisher=PHP Institute|isbn=978-4569669304|language=Japanese}}{{cite book|title=Taiyō no chizuchō 24 zenkoku 'Ichinomiya' meguri|last1=Okada|first1=Shoji|date=2014|publisher=Heibonsha|isbn=978-4582945614|language=Japanese}} Those two deities and their son {{ill|Ame-no-Oshikumone|ja|天押雲根命|en|draft:Ame-no-Oshikumone|simple|User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|fr|Utilisateur:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Oshikumone|qq=}}{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} are ancestors of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan|qq=}} and {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}.Shibata, Joue. Saitama Sōsho. (1929) Volume 1: Chichibu Shi, p 111, Chichibu hikomikoto o keizu 『埼玉叢書. 第1巻』内『秩父志』内111頁「秩父彦命御系図」. Sanmeisha{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|last=Ten Grotenhuis|first=Elizabeth|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} {{ill|Hiraoka Shrine|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hiraoka Shrine|qq=}} is located in the western foothills of the {{ill|Mount Ikoma|lt=Ikoma Mountains|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mount Ikoma|qq=}} in central {{ill|Osaka Prefecture|en|Osaka Prefecture|qid=Q122723|lt=Osaka Prefecture|1=Osaka Prefecture}}. In its earliest days, it was a center for {{ill|Mountain worship|en|Mountain worship|qid=Q93697439|lt=mountain worship|1=Mountain worship}} and the ''[[kami|kami]]'' of Kozudake, the peak immediately behind the shrine, came to be identified with {{ill|Ame-no-Koyane|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ame-no-Koyane|qq=}}, the tutelary deity of the {{ill|Nakatomi clan|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakatomi clan|qq=}}, the ancestors of the {{ill|Fujiwara clan|en|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fujiwara clan|qq=}}. == Components == He has five components each of which has a corresponding Buddha. Four original members and then the fifth member
